# Results — Study 679 (Psychological Line)

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The claim under test — the
Japanese **Psychological Line**, PSY(12) = 100 x (up-closes in the last 12 days) / 12, is an
overbought/oversold gauge: **PSY > 75 -> sell** ("everyone who wants to buy already has"),
**PSY < 25 -> buy** ("everyone who wants to sell already has"). One documented execution lag
throughout: PSY is known from closes up to and including bar *t*; every trade / forward-return
window enters at bar *t+1*'s **open** and exits at the close of bar *t+h*. Offline & deterministic
once cached; run `python examples/verify.py` to reproduce every number. As-of **2026-06-30**
(the last complete calendar month). Fingerprints below.

Total-return (`auto_adjust=True`) daily OHLC, yfinance, no key. **No survivorship on SPY/QQQ/IWM**
(index ETFs). **Named on the Signal axis:** the single-name sleeve (AAPL, TSLA, NVDA) is three
well-known, currently-thriving mega caps chosen for liquidity — not a systematically-selected
historical panel. A milder bias than a "top-N by market cap today" cross-sectional basket, but
worth saying out loud: a 2003-vintage tech basket that kept its era's flame-outs would likely
look different.

## The headline — forward return conditioned on the PSY(12) reading, pooled universe

One documented execution lag: PSY known at close *t*, forward return entered at *t+1*'s open,
exited at the close of *t+5* (5 trading days held). **Trigger events only** — the day PSY first
crosses *into* a zone, not every day inside it (PSY is a rolling window; scoring every in-zone day
pools heavily-overlapping, non-independent observations and inflates significance — see the
robustness note below). Welch *t* is the planned primary (near non-overlapping single events);
Newey-West (5 lags) is the residual overlap cross-check (the 5-day forward windows themselves
still overlap a little near a cluster of triggers).

| PSY bucket | n | mean fwd. return (bps / 5d) | Welch *t* (vs neutral) | NW(5) *t* |
|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| oversold, PSY < 25 ("buy") | 97 | **+159.13** | +1.32 | +1.64 |
| neutral (all other trigger-free days) | 33,074 | +45.87 | — | — |
| overbought, PSY > 75 ("sell") | 398 | +66.09 | +1.04 | +1.10 |

**Neither leg clears the desk's t >= 2 bar.** The oversold point estimate is directionally
right (+159 bps vs +46 bps neutral) but n = 97 is small and noisy (t = 1.32). The overbought
point estimate is directionally **wrong** for the claim — PSY > 75 is followed by *more*
positive drift (+66 bps), not a decline — though, again, not statistically distinguishable
from the neutral bucket (t = 1.04). All three buckets sit on the positive side because the
20-year sample rides a secular bull market; PSY conditioning does not visibly change that.
**Per-instrument check:** every single ticker's own Welch *t* (low and high separately) is
also |*t*| < 2 — SPY (−0.20 / +0.60), QQQ (+1.71 / −1.28), IWM (+0.37 / +0.57), AAPL
(+0.63 / +0.41), TSLA (+1.10 / +1.21), NVDA (−0.08 / +0.68). No instrument carries a
certifiable edge either way.

## The timer — zone-trigger trade ledger vs a random-direction control

Actually trade it: long on an oversold trigger, short on an overbought trigger, enter next
open, hold 5 trading days, one-way cost x NAV x 2 legs per round trip. Pinned against a
**random-direction control** on the identical entry bars and dates (the "beats a coin?"
myth-check) — same n, same timing, only the sign of the bet is randomized (seed 679).

| cost (one-way) | arm | n | win rate | mean (bps/trade) | HAC *t* |
|---|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 5.0 bps | **PSY timer** | 495 | 41.0% | **−31.95** | **−1.49** |
| 5.0 bps | random-direction (coin) | 495 | 50.3% | +18.57 | +0.69 |
| 10.0 bps | **PSY timer** | 495 | 39.6% | **−41.95** | **−1.95** |
| 10.0 bps | random-direction (coin) | 495 | 48.7% | +8.57 | +0.32 |

Delta (PSY timer − coin, cost-invariant since both arms pay the identical cost): **−50.52
bps/trade**, Welch *t* = **−1.55**. The point estimate favors the coin by a wide margin —
the contrarian rule loses money on net while a same-bar random bet does not — but the gap
does **not** clear the certification bar (|*t*| < 2), so we call it a lean, not a verdict.
At 10 bps the PSY timer alone edges to *t* = −1.95, a hair short of the bar.

## Parameter robustness — window x (oversold, overbought), conditional-split Welch *t*

The textbook recipe (window = 12, thresholds 25/75, highlighted) sits squarely inside the
noise band on **both** legs. A few off-textbook corners of the grid cross |*t*| >= 2 on the
oversold leg alone (window 12/[30,70]: *t* = +2.47; window 20/[25,75]: *t* = +2.60; window
20/[30,70]: *t* = +2.17) — exactly the shape of a parameter-mined false positive, not a
robust effect: none of those corners was the pre-registered rule, none survives on the
overbought leg, and the *n* shrinks sharply as the window grows (window 20 has as few as 0–66
oversold events on the whole 23-year tape). We also note window 10 and 12 both reproduce
*identical* low-bucket counts across adjacent threshold pairs — PSY(*N*) only takes steps of
100/*N* %, so thresholds that don't straddle a step (e.g. 25 and 30 with window = 10, whose
only achievable values near there are 20 and 30) select the *same* set of days. A robustness
sweep on a discretized indicator needs threshold choices wide enough to actually move the
achievable-value grid — a footgun worth naming.

| window | zone | n low | Welch *t* low | n high | Welch *t* high |
|--:|---|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 10 | [20, 80] | 57 | +1.29 | 234 | +1.15 |
| 10 | [25, 75] | 354 | +1.33 | 949 | +1.30 |
| 10 | [30, 70] | 354 | +1.33 | 949 | +1.30 |
| **12** | **[20, 80]** | 97 | +1.32 | 398 | +1.04 |
| **12** | **[25, 75] (textbook)** | **97** | **+1.32** | **398** | **+1.04** |
| 12 | [30, 70] | 454 | +2.47 | 1,175 | +0.87 |
| 14 | [20, 80] | 19 | +0.53 | 162 | +0.79 |
| 14 | [25, 75] | 134 | +0.80 | 567 | −0.35 |
| 14 | [30, 70] | 534 | +1.72 | 1,373 | +0.49 |
| 20 | [20, 80] | 0 | n/a | 31 | +0.55 |
| 20 | [25, 75] | 13 | +2.60 | 158 | +0.30 |
| 20 | [30, 70] | 66 | +2.17 | 427 | +0.98 |

## Synthetic positive control — the machinery is unbiased

Deterministic tape: i.i.d. daily noise plus a drift that switches on exactly when *that
day's* PSY(12) reading (computed causally) sits in the tested zone — a positive kicker after
oversold, a negative kicker after overbought, the literal claim planted on the literal
condition. Each seed pools a 6-series synthetic basket (mirrors the real 6-ticker universe;
a lone synthetic path gives too few oversold/overbought events for a stable Welch *t*). A
`min_gap` cooldown equal to the hold period keeps trigger events non-overlapping, on the real
tape and the synthetic tape alike — omitting it (every in-zone day, no cooldown) inflates the
real headline's noise-world false-positive rate from ~5% to 20–30% across seeds, which is why
the trigger design above uses it.

| world | *t* (oversold leg) | *t* (overbought leg) |
|---|--:|--:|
| null (reversal = 0), **20 seeds** | mean **−0.19** (sd 1.02), \|*t*\|>=2 in **1/20** seeds | mean **−0.19** (sd 1.13), \|*t*\|>=2 in **1/20** seeds |
| planted reversal = +0.006/day (seed 679) | **+7.03** | **−7.47** |

The detector sits at the nominal false-positive rate on the null (1/20 seeds, matching the
expected ~5%) and lights up hard on a planted effect the same size and shape as the claim.
The real tape's flat result above is not a broken harness.

## Verdict

- **Signal — NONE.** Neither the oversold leg (+159 bps/5d, Welch *t* = +1.32, NW *t* =
  +1.64) nor the overbought leg (+66 bps/5d, Welch *t* = +1.04, NW *t* = +1.10) clears
  *t* >= 2 on the real tape, every one of the six instruments individually is |*t*| < 2 both
  ways, and the overbought leg's point estimate runs the *wrong* direction for the claim
  (more positive, not negative). The handful of parameter-grid corners that cross the bar are
  off-textbook and one-sided — a data-mining shape, not a robust effect.
- **Tradability — MIRAGE.** The zone-trigger timer loses **−31.95 bps/trade net** (5 bps
  cost, HAC *t* = −1.49), worse at 10 bps (**−41.95 bps**, *t* = −1.95). No cost level makes
  it money; the loss only deepens.
- **"Beats a coin?" — MIXED.** The random-direction control on identical entry bars earns
  **+18.57 bps/trade** where the PSY timer loses **−31.95** — a **50.52 bps/trade** gap
  favoring the coin — but the gap's own Welch *t* (−1.55) does not clear the certification
  bar. Directionally the coin wins; statistically we can't fully certify it.
